b: Glucagon is a peptide hormone secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreas. It serves as an antagonist to insulin and plays a vital role in increasing blood glucose levels, particularly during fasting or starvation.
Mobilizes fuel by promoting glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver.
Increases fatty acid release from adipose tissue by promoting triglyceride breakdown.
It acts through the cAMP second messenger system.

qs.q: Why is glucagon specifically effective in managing severe beta-blocker overdose?
o: It activates adenyl cyclase via a mechanism bypassing beta receptors
It directly stimulates peripheral alpha-2 vasoconstriction
It blocks calcium influx through L-type myocardial channels
It increases renal potassium excretion to correct arrhythmias
qs.e: Glucagon directly increases cardiac inotropy by activating adenyl cyclase via a secondary mechanism separate from catecholamines, effectively bypassing beta blockade. Catecholamines are often less effective due to the blocked receptors.

qs.q: Which of the following is an effect of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)?
o: It stimulates secretion of gastric acid.
It suppresses insulin release.
It enhances glucagon secretion.
It delays gastric emptying.
qs.e: GLP-1 is an incretin hormone released from intestinal L cells. Its key actions include stimulating glucose-dependent insulin secretion, inhibiting glucagon secretion, and slowing gastric emptying, all of which contribute to lowering post-prandial blood glucose levels. It also inhibits gastric acid secretion.

ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Glucagon is a pancreatic alpha‑cell hormone that raises blood glucose by stimulating liver glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, acting as a counter‑regulatory partner to insulin. It also mobilises fatty acids from adipose tissue via cAMP signalling.

sections.p: Glucagon is a 29‑amino‑acid peptide produced by pancreatic alpha cells. It is released when blood glucose falls, acting to restore normoglycaemia by stimulating hepatic glucose output and lipolysis.

Glucagon binds the G‑protein coupled GLP‑1 receptor on hepatocytes, activating adenylate cyclase, raising cAMP, and triggering protein kinase A. This phosphorylates enzymes that promote glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis, and activates hormone‑sensitive lipase in adipose tissue.
Secretion rises during hypoglycaemia, prolonged fasting, or exercise. It falls after meals when insulin rises. Sympathetic stimulation and low glucose directly stimulate alpha cells.

Excess glucagon causes glucagonoma (neuroendocrine tumour) with hyperglycaemia, weight loss, and necrolytic migratory erythema. Deficiency is rare but can contribute to severe hypoglycaemia in insulin‑treated diabetics.
In hypoglycaemic emergencies, glucagon is administered IM or SC when oral glucose is unavailable. It is also used diagnostically to confirm insulin deficiency or in insulin‑related hypoglycaemia.

t.b: High glucagon in hypoglycaemia indicates counter‑regulatory response; low levels suggest alpha‑cell failure or insulinoma.
Failure to rise after glucagon indicates hepatic glycogen depletion or severe liver disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypoglycaemia unresponsive to oral glucose
Unexplained weight loss with hyperglycaemia and skin rash

faq.q: Why is glucagon given when a patient cannot swallow?
faq.a: It raises blood glucose by stimulating liver glycogenolysis without needing intestinal absorption.
No; it increases glucose. However, if given too late after insulin overdose, the rise may be insufficient.

faq.q: What is the difference between glucagon and epinephrine in hypoglycaemia?
faq.a: Both raise glucose; epinephrine also increases heart rate and vasoconstriction, while glucagon acts mainly on the liver.
